title: Pages that read chats, and the management page inside the app

steps.page: Pages that can read your chats
steps.intro: Your goal 2: any page can list chats and offer a Resume button, behind the usual approval card.

steps.path: A page's approval card, and what the page can see
steps.headline: When you approve a page to read your chats, how much should it see?
steps.today: Pages can keep their own small data file, call approved web services, and since Oct 14 open the new-chat window. They cannot see any of your chats. Each chat already has a name, last-active date, tags, a note, its project folder, its model, and pinned/complete marks.
steps.problem: A page that can't see chats can't show 'which chats worked on this' or offer Resume. But a chat list is personal: a page from the marketplace could show your chat names to whatever web service it's also approved to reach.
steps.proposal: The page names what it wants in its settings file; the approval card says it in plain words ('Read your chat list: names, dates, tags, notes and projects'), like the existing cards. Pick how wide one approval reaches.

options.label: The page names its scope
options.summary: A page asks for all chats, chats in named projects, or chats with a named tag. The card shows exactly that, and you approve or refuse it.
pros: The management page asks for everything; a small project page asks for just its project.
You see the exact reach before saying yes.
cons: Slightly more wording on the approval card.

options.label: All chats or none
options.summary: One approval lets the page see every chat.
pros: Simplest card and simplest to build.
cons: A page that only needs one project still sees everything.

steps.path: What a chat-reading page can do
steps.headline: Should an approved page also be able to change chats, or only read them and offer Resume?
steps.today: In the app you can rename a chat, tag it, write a note, and mark it pinned or complete. Resume opens a past chat, or jumps to it if it's already open.
steps.problem: Letting pages change chats is more powerful, but a faulty page could rename or retag many chats at once.

options.label: Read and Resume only
options.summary: Pages see chats and can offer Resume, which only works after a real click, the same rule as Start a chat. Nothing on a chat can be changed.
pros: Nothing a page does can damage your chat list.
Enough for the management page: items record which chats belong to them, not the other way round.
cons: Tagging or noting a chat from a page waits for a later round.

options.label: Also change tags and notes
options.summary: A second, separate approval lets a page set tags, notes and marks.
pros: A page could tag chats by work item for you.
cons: More to build and test now.
A faulty page could mislabel many chats.

steps.path: The chat list a page sees
steps.headline: Two facts the chat list lacks today get added: the branch a chat worked on, and whether it is open right now.
steps.changed: Stated, not asked: the app records each chat's branch in its files but never shows it, and the past-chats list leaves out chats that are open. Both get added so a page can match chats to work items and show 'Working' only when a chat is really open.
steps.notice: The management page's 'Working' marker stops guessing from recent saves and becomes true only while a chat on that item is open. The app's own past-chats screen looks the same.

steps.page: Keeping the management page up to date
steps.intro: Your goal 3: chats keep the page true as they start, pause and finish work.

steps.path: The start and end of every work chat
steps.headline: Should every work chat join an item at its start and close it automatically at merge?
steps.today: Chats don't record themselves on items. Only 11 of 144 items are linked to any branch, by hand. Marking an item Merged is a command someone has to remember to run.
steps.problem: 'Several chats on one item' can't be tracked if chats don't say which item they're on, and an item stays unfinished after its work merges unless someone remembers.
steps.proposal: Yes: at its start a work chat finds the matching item (or proposes a new one the idea-intake way and waits for your yes), names its branch after it (for example 75-project-skills) and records itself on it. Wrap-up writes the item's progress note (done / next / blocked). Pausing records the reason. Merging moves the item to Merged on its own. No: items stay hand-linked.

steps.headline: Where should changes to the work items be saved?
steps.today: Items live on this session's branch. The page saves each bulk edit to whatever branch the copy it runs from is on.
steps.problem: After merging, the only copy on master is the shared folder, which refuses all saves by design, so bulk edit would fail. And while chats edit items on their own branches, each sees a different list until it merges.
steps.proposal: Pick where item changes are saved.

options.label: Straight to master
options.summary: One dedicated copy of master saves item changes and pushes them at once, with no pull request. The page and every chat save through it.
pros: The page and every chat see the same list within seconds.
Item changes never clash when work merges.
Bulk edit keeps working after merge.
cons: Item edits skip the pull request step (they are bookkeeping, not app code).
A wrong bulk Delete reaches master at once; history can undo it, but no button does yet.

options.label: On each chat's branch
options.summary: As now: an item change travels with that chat's work.
pros: Item changes are reviewed with their work.
cons: The page shows a stale or partial list.
Bulk edit fails from master.

steps.path: The 'Merge to master' button on an item
steps.headline: What should 'Merge to master' do when pressed?
steps.today: The button shows when an item's pull request passes its checks, and only says 'not built yet'. A real merge means: merge, push, run the close-out checks, archive the plan documents, mark the item Merged, and remove its copies and branches.
steps.problem: Done half-way, it leaves stale copies of work and an item still showing as unfinished.

options.label: Opens a chat that merges
options.summary: Opens the new-chat window with 'Merge item #75 to master' filled in. You press Start, and the chat does every step and reports back.
pros: Every step runs, with the same checks as when you ask in chat.
If something fails, the chat explains and can fix it.
cons: One extra click, and about a minute.

options.label: The page merges itself
options.summary: The page merges directly after a confirmation.
pros: One click, seconds.
cons: Cleanup gets rebuilt in the page, a second copy that can drift.
A failure mid-way leaves a half-done state.

steps.intro: You asked for the management page to be built into YouCoded. These two decide what that means.

steps.path: The Pages list in the app
steps.headline: Who should see the built-in management page?
steps.today: The app has one built-in page, Office, listed only when Office is set up. Everyone else's pages are folders they made. The management page reads the cards/ folder of your YouCoded workspace, its branches and its pull requests.
steps.problem: YouCoded is for students and everyday users too. Shipped to everyone as-is, they'd see a page about YouCoded's own development, or an empty one.

options.label: Shown where items exist
options.summary: Built in, but listed only for a project that has a cards/ folder, as Office is listed only when set up. Today that's just your workspace.
pros: Ships with the app, as you asked.
Invisible to everyone else until a project of theirs uses items.
A later step could let any project use items.
cons: Checks for the folder on each project.

options.label: Shown to everyone
options.summary: Every install lists it.
pros: Simplest.
cons: Most people see a page that means nothing to them.

options.label: Your own page, not built in
options.summary: It lives in your Pages folder only; the app ships only the abilities it uses.
pros: Nothing new in the app for other people.
cons: Not what you asked for.
Only on computers where that folder syncs.

steps.path: How the built-in page is made
steps.headline: Should the built-in page use the same abilities as any other page, or be part of the app's own screens?
steps.today: Office, the one built-in page, is part of the app's own screens. The management page today is a separate web page drawn by a small program, in the app's look.
steps.problem: Built into the app's own screens, it can do anything but proves nothing about what other pages can do. Made as a normal page, it needs abilities pages don't have yet: reading chats (goal 2) and reading and saving work items.

options.label: A page, using page abilities
options.summary: It ships with the app but runs like any page: it reads chats with the new ability, and items and their branches with a second new one limited to the cards/ folder. Your approved design carries over.
pros: Every ability it needs becomes available to any page, as you want for goal 2.
It is the first real test of those abilities.
The approved design carries over almost as-is.
cons: Two new abilities to build, approve and test.
Saving items still needs the app to save and push to GitHub on the page's behalf.

options.label: Part of the app's own screens
options.summary: Rebuilt in the app's own screen code, like Office.
pros: No new page abilities needed for it.
cons: The whole design is rebuilt from scratch.
Goal 2's chat ability gets no real user.

steps.intro: When things merge, and what to do with the snapshot sections and old copies of work.

steps.headline: Should the items and the current page merge soon, with goals 2 and 3 built afterwards on new branches?
steps.today: Nothing is merged. Master has changed the old roadmap files three times since this branch started; this branch deletes them. 14 other branches still edit the old roadmap. A trial merge shows 4 small clashes.
steps.problem: Every day unmerged, chats keep writing roadmap entries that must be moved into items again, and an old branch merging later would quietly bring the roadmap files back.

options.label: Merge items soon
options.summary: After you approve the sorting deck: bring master's changes in, move its 2 new roadmap entries into items, add a check that refuses roadmap files coming back, verify, then ask you 'ready to merge?'. Goals 2 and 3 follow as separate merges.
pros: Clashes stop growing; every chat starts filing items.
Each later piece is small enough to judge on its own.
cons: Until goals 2 and 3 land, the page keeps its 'not built yet' buttons. Only you see it.

options.label: Finish everything first
options.summary: Build goals 2 and 3 on this branch, then merge once.
pros: One merge.
cons: Clashes grow daily.
A very large merge is harder to check and to undo.

steps.path: Screens, Big picture and Tidy up, and the 'Facts as of Oct 12' header
steps.headline: What should happen to the sections still showing the Oct 12 snapshot?
steps.today: Today is live from the items. Screens, Big picture and Tidy up still show a copy made Oct 12, and the header dates the whole page Oct 12. Item #147 already covers redoing Screens.
steps.problem: A page mixing live and old facts under one date can't be trusted at a glance.
steps.proposal: Two ways, as part of building the in-app page.

options.label: Make two live
options.summary: Big picture reads the items directly; Tidy up reads idle copies of work live. Screens keeps its own 'Pictures from Oct 12' date until #147. The header date goes.
pros: Everything but Screens is current every time you open it.
cons: More work before the page is done.

options.label: Label them, wait for #147
options.summary: Each snapshot section gets its own date line; nothing else changes.
pros: Quick and honest.
cons: Big picture and Tidy up drift further out of date.

steps.surface: Copies of work on this computer
steps.headline: What should happen to the 9 copies of work idle 2+ weeks and never merged?
steps.today: 9 folders (model picker tags, per-project skills, three specialist-plan copies, theme plugin update, usage visibility, two old plan comparisons) were last touched Sept 11 to 29. All have unsaved changes; most hold work never merged.
steps.problem: They show up as unfinished work every chat, but some may hold the only copy of something you'd want.

options.label: Decide one by one
options.summary: A deck, one row per copy: what it was, what's unsaved, which item it belongs to. Clean means back up every change to GitHub first, then remove the folder.
pros: Nothing lost by accident.
cons: One more deck.

options.label: Back up and clean all
options.summary: Every unsaved change is pushed to GitHub on its branch, then all 9 folders are removed.
pros: One step; the work stays on GitHub.
cons: Old half-done changes get pushed unread.

options.label: Keep them all
options.summary: Leave them.
pros: No risk.
cons: The warning keeps appearing every chat.
